claim: IFNγ stimulation of J2 virus transformed bone marrow-derived macrophages for 24 hours results in upregulation of MHCII, CD40, and PD-L1 on the cell surface.
source: Stimulation of these macrophages with IFNγ for 24 hours resulted in the upregulation of T cell stimulatory molecules, MHCII and CD40, and the inhibitory ligand PD-L1 (Cd274), on the cell surface (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: sgRNAs targeting H2-Ab1, Cd40, or Cd274 were significantly depleted from cell populations expressing the targeted surface molecule.
source: When the abundances of sgRNAs specific for H2-Ab1 (encoding the MHCII, H2-I-A beta chain), Cd40, or Cd274 (PD-L1) were compared between high- and low-expressing cell populations, we found that each of these sgRNAs were significantly depleted from the cell populations expressing the targeted surface molecule, while each had no consistent effect on the expression of non-targeted genes (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the CRISPR screen shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Targeting genes for respective surface markers altered mean relative abundance 30-60-fold in the CRISPR screens.
source: While not all individual sgRNAs produced an identical effect, we found that targeting the genes that served as the basis of sorting altered the mean relative abundance 30–60-fold, demonstrating that all selections efficiently differentiated responsive from non-responsive cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of sgRNA enrichment data from the screens.

claim: TNF stimulation enhances IFNγ-mediated CD40 expression in macrophages.
source: Previous studies suggested that TNF stimulation enhances IFNγ-mediated CD40 expression in hematopoietic progenitors (Gu et al., 2012), and we confirmed this observation in macrophages (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1E and cites previous literature.

claim: A six-fold higher induction of CD40 was observed in macrophages stimulated with a combination of IFNγ and TNF compared to IFNγ alone.
source: We observed a six-fold higher induction of CD40 in macrophages stimulated with a combination of IFNγ and TNF compared to IFNγ alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing CD40 induction under different stimulation conditions.

claim: TNF does not enhance IFNγ-induced MHCII expression.
source: This synergy was specific to CD40 induction as we did not observe any enhancement of IFNγ-induced MHCII expression by TNF addition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects of TNF on CD40 versus MHCII.

claim: Mutation of Ostc and Cnbp enhances IFNγ-dependent induction of PD-L1 surface levels.
source: We generated KO macrophages for each of these novel candidates and confirmed that mutation of these genes enhances the IFNγ-dependent induction of PD-L1 surface levels (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The most important positive regulators of the IFNγ response correspond to the proximal IFNγ signaling complex.
source: The most important positive regulators corresponded to the proximal IFNγ signaling complex (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined analysis of CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Known negative regulators of IFNγ signaling include Pias1, Ptpn2, Mapk1, Socs1, and Socs3.
source: Similarly, we identified known negative regulators of IFNγ signaling, including the protein inhibitor of activated Stat1 (Pias1) (Liu et al., 1998), protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 2 (Ptpn2) (Manguso et al., 2017), mitogen activate protein kinase 1 (Mapk1), and suppressor of cytokine signaling 1 (Socs1) and 3 (Socs3).
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR screen data and cites previous literature for known regulators.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis identified mitochondrial respiration and oxidative phosphorylation pathways as enriched among positive regulators of the IFNγ response.
source: GSEA identified a similarly robust enrichment for gene sets related to mitochondrial respiration and oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis of the combined CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Gene sets dedicated to the assembly and function of complex I of the mitochondrial respiratory chain were significantly enriched.
source: In particular, we found a significant enrichment of gene sets dedicated to the assembly and function of the NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductose (hereafter, 'complex I') of the mitochondrial respiratory chain.
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis of the CRISPR screen data.

claim: Disruption of almost every subunit of complex I impaired the response to IFNγ, with the exception of Ndufab1.
source: This analysis failed to demonstrate a clear role for sgRNAs targeting components of complexes II, III, or IV in the expression of the IFNγ-inducible surface markers tested. In contrast, the disruption of almost every subunit of complex I impaired the response to IFNγ, with the notable exception of Ndufab1.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of individual ETC complex components in the CRISPR screen data.

claim: Ndufab1 is essential for viability.
source: As this gene is essential for viability (Stroud et al., 2016), we assume that cells carrying Ndufab1 sgRNAs retain functional target protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Of the 42 individual assembly factors or structural subunits of complex I present in the mutant library, 29 were significantly enriched as positive regulators in the global analysis.
source: Of the 42 individual assembly factors or structural subunits of complex I present in our mutant library, 29 were significantly enriched as positive regulators in the global analysis and were generally required for the induction of all IFNγ-inducible markers (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is a significant correlation between the magnitude of enrichment in the genetic screen and a subunit's effect on the structural stability of the N-module.
source: For a given subunit, we found a significant correlation between the magnitude of enrichment in our genetic screen and its effect on the structural stability of the module (Figure 2E), specifically implicating the activity of complex I in the IFNγ response.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis comparing genetic screen data with proteomic data, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: IFNγ or TLR2 stimulation with Pam3CSK4 produced similar overall metabolic effects, increasing both OCR and ECAR in macrophages.
source: IFNγ or toll-like receptor (TLR) 2 stimulation with Pam3CSK4 produced similar overall metabolic effects, increasing both OCR and ECAR in these cells (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse metabolic measurements shown in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: IFNγ increased both the basal and maximal oxygen consumption rate in macrophages.
source: Further analysis of mitochondrial function revealed that IFNγ increased both the basal and maximal OCR that was observed upon decoupling electron transport from ATP generation (Figure 2H) with carbonyl cyanide-4-trifluoromethoxy phenylhydrazone (FCCP).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse metabolic measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: When cultured in media containing glucose, all cell lines (sgNTC, sgNdufa1, sgNdufa2) produced equivalent amounts of ATP.
source: When cultured in media containing the glycolytic substrate, glucose, all cell lines produced equivalent amounts of ATP (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When pyruvate was provided as the sole carbon source, sgNdufa1 and sgNdufa2 macrophages contained decreased ATP levels compared to sgNTC cells.
source: However, when pyruvate was provided as the sole carbon source and ATP generation depended entirely upon flux through ETC and OXPHOS, both sgNdufa1 and sgNdufa2 macrophages contained decreased ATP levels compared to sgNTC cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Oligomycin reduced ATP levels in sgNTC macrophages but had no effect in sgNdufa1 and sgNdufa2 cells.
source: While oligomycin reduced ATP levels in sgNTC macrophages, this treatment had no effect in sgNdufa1 and sgNdufa2 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), confirming that these complex I-deficient cells rely on glycolysis for energy generation.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Complex I-deficient cells rely on glycolysis for energy generation.
source: While oligomycin reduced ATP levels in sgNTC macrophages, this treatment had no effect in sgNdufa1 and sgNdufa2 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), confirming that these complex I-deficient cells rely on glycolysis for energy generation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects of oligomycin on ATP levels.

claim: Mutation of complex I genes significantly reduced the IFNγ-dependent induction of MHCII and PD-L1 compared to sgNTC.
source: Also consistent with predictions, mutation of complex I genes significantly reduced the IFNγ-dependent induction of MHCII and PD-L1 compared to sgNTC (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3C-F.

claim: The Ndufa1 mutation that abolishes OXPHOS reduced MHCII induction to the same level as Ifngr1-deficient cells.
source: The Ndufa1 mutation that abolishes OXPHOS reduced MHCII induction to the same level as Ifngr1-deficient cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of MHCII induction levels between different mutant cell lines.

claim: Rotenone treatment caused a dose-dependent inhibition of IFNγ-induced MHCII expression in sgNTC macrophages.
source: This treatment caused a dose-dependent inhibition of the IFNγ-induced MHCII expression in sgNTC macrophages (Figure 3G) and had a similar inhibitory effect on the residual IFNγ response in Ndufa2-deficient cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Complex I is required for the induction of immunomodulatory surface molecules in response to IFNγ.
source: Together, these results confirm that complex I is required for the induction of immunomodulatory surface molecules in response to IFNγ.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including genetic and chemical inhibition studies.

claim: Oligomycin inhibited IFNγ-induced MHCII expression, albeit to a lesser extent than rotenone.
source: The complex V inhibitor, oligomycin, inhibited the IFNγ-induced MHCII expression, albeit to a lesser extent than direct complex I inhibition with rotenone (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing effects of different inhibitors shown in Figure 3H.

claim: CCCP had no effect on the IFNγ response, indicating that ATP generation is dispensable for IFNγ responsiveness.
source: CCCP had no effect on the IFNγ response, indicating that ATP generation is dispensable for IFNγ responsiveness and highlighting a specific role for complex I activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no effect of CCCP on IFNγ-induced MHCII expression.

claim: Treatment with antimycin A or sodium azide had less effect on IFNγ-mediated MHCII expression than rotenone treatment.
source: While treatment with these inhibitors lowered ATP concentration similarly to rotenone in glucose-containing media (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), the effect of complex III or IV inhibition on IFNγ-mediated MHCII expression was less than rotenone treatment and was similar to the partial inhibition observed with oligomycin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing effects of different ETC inhibitors shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: IFNγ stimulated MHCII expression to a similar degree in macrophages cultured in complete media with glucose as in media containing only pyruvate or citrate.
source: IFNγ was found to stimulate MHCII expression to a similar degree in macrophages cultured in complete media with glucose as in media containing only pyruvate or citrate, which must be catabolized via mitochondrial respiration (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing MHCII induction in different media conditions shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Cellular respiration is both necessary and sufficient for maximal expression of the IFNγ-inducible surface markers MHCII and PD-L1.
source: Taken together these results suggest that cellular respiration is both necessary and sufficient for maximal expression of the IFNγ-inducible surface markers MHCII and PD-L1.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results testing different carbon sources and inhibitors.

claim: sgNdufa1 and sgNdufa2 mutant macrophages secreted larger amounts of TNF and IL-6 than sgNTC cells in response to Pam3CSK4.
source: Indeed, not only were TLR responses intact in sgNdufa1 and sgNdufa2 mutant macrophages, these cells secreted larger amounts of TNF or interleukin 6 (IL-6) than sgNTC cells in response to the TLR2 ligand, Pam3CSK4. (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The glycolytic dependency of complex I-deficient cells enhanced the TLR2 response.
source: Thus, the glycolytic dependency of these cells enhanced the TLR2 response, indicating opposing metabolic dependencies for IFNγ and TLR signaling.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the observation that complex I-deficient cells have enhanced TLR2 responses.

claim: IFNγ and TLR signaling have opposing metabolic dependencies.
source: Thus, the glycolytic dependency of these cells enhanced the TLR2 response, indicating opposing metabolic dependencies for IFNγ and TLR signaling.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from comparing the metabolic requirements of IFNγ and TLR responses.

claim: Linezolid treatment produced a cell line with ~50% fewer mitochondrial genomes per nuclear genome compared to control cells.
source: This treatment produced a cell line with ~50% fewer mitochondrial genomes per nuclear genome and a corresponding decrease in OXPHOS capacity compared to control cells grown in the absence of LZD (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Reduction in mitochondrial mass nearly abrogated the IFNγ-dependent induction of MHCII.
source: Consistent with our complex I inhibition studies, we found that this reduction in mitochondrial mass nearly abrogated the IFNγ-dependent induction of MHCII (Figure 4D), while the TLR2-dependent secretion of TNF and IL-6 was preserved or enhanced (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: TLR2-dependent secretion of TNF and IL-6 was preserved or enhanced in cells with reduced mitochondrial mass.
source: Consistent with our complex I inhibition studies, we found that this reduction in mitochondrial mass nearly abrogated the IFNγ-dependent induction of MHCII (Figure 4D), while the TLR2-dependent secretion of TNF and IL-6 was preserved or enhanced (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figures 4E and F.

claim: Mitochondrial activity is necessary for a robust IFNγ response.
source: Thus, mitochondrial activity, itself, is necessary for a robust IFNγ response.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing reduced IFNγ responses in cells with reduced mitochondrial mass.

claim: Replacing glucose with galactose had no effect on IFNγ-induced MHCII induction.
source: Inhibition of ROS generation by replacing glucose with galactose (Wang et al., 2018; Brand and Nicholls, 2011; Bustamante et al., 1978) had no effect on IFNγ-induced MHCII induction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data testing the role of ROS in the IFNγ response.

claim: Neutralization of cytosolic or mitochondrial radicals with NAC or MitoTEMPO had no effect on MHCII induction.
source: Similarly, neutralization of cytosolic or mitochondrial radicals with N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) or MitoTEMPO, respectively, had no effect on MHCII induction either alone or in combination with ETC inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data testing the role of ROS in the IFNγ response.

claim: Stabilizing HIF-1α with DMOG did not affect IFNγ-induced MHCII cell surface expression.
source: The role of the cytosolic redox sensor, HIF-1α (Cramer et al., 2003; Semenza, 2012), was addressed by chemically stabilizing this factor with dimethyloxalylglycine (DMOG). A potential role for nitric oxide production was addressed with the specific NOS2 inhibitor 1400W (Everts et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018; Braverman and Stanley, 2017). Neither of these treatments affected IFNγ-induced MHCII cell surface expression in the presence or absence of simultaneous Pam3CSK4, further supporting a direct relationship between mitochondrial respiratory capacity and the IFNγ response.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data testing the role of HIF-1α in the IFNγ response.

claim: Inhibiting NOS2 with 1400W did not affect IFNγ-induced MHCII cell surface expression.
source: The role of the cytosolic redox sensor, HIF-1α (Cramer et al., 2003; Semenza, 2012), was addressed by chemically stabilizing this factor with dimethyloxalylglycine (DMOG). A potential role for nitric oxide production was addressed with the specific NOS2 inhibitor 1400W (Everts et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018; Braverman and Stanley, 2017). Neither of these treatments affected IFNγ-induced MHCII cell surface expression in the presence or absence of simultaneous Pam3CSK4, further supporting a direct relationship between mitochondrial respiratory capacity and the IFNγ response.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data testing the role of nitric oxide in the IFNγ response.

claim: Rotenone inhibited the IFNγ-mediated induction of PD-L1, ICAM1, and CD40 in human GM-CSF-derived macrophages.
source: As seen in the murine model, rotenone inhibited the IFNγ-mediated induction of all three markers (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from human cells shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Rotenone significantly enhanced the secretion of IL-1β and TNF upon Pam3CSK4 stimulation of human GM-CSF-derived macrophages.
source: Upon Pam3CSK4 stimulation of GM-CSF-derived MDM, rotenone significantly enhanced the secretion of IL-1β and TNF (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data from human cells shown in Figures 5B and C.

claim: Complex I is specifically required for IFNγ signaling in human macrophages.
source: Thus, as we observed in mouse cells, complex I is specifically required for IFNγ signaling in human macrophages.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from experiments in human cells showing differential effects of rotenone on IFNγ versus TLR2 responses.

claim: Both mRNA and protein expression of PD-L1 and MHCII were diminished to a similar degree in sgNdufa1 and sgNdufa2 compared to sgNTC cells.
source: In both cases, mRNA induction preceded surface expression of the respective protein. More importantly, both mRNA and protein expression of each marker were diminished to a similar degree in sgNdufa1 and sgNdufa2 compared to sgNTC cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by time course data comparing mRNA and protein levels shown in Figures 6A and B.

claim: A deficit in transcriptional induction accounts for the decrease in surface expression observed in complex I deficient cells.
source: Thus, a deficit in transcriptional induction could account for the subsequent decrease in surface expression observed in complex I deficient cells.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the observation that both mRNA and protein are reduced in complex I-deficient cells.

claim: As the addition of rotenone was delayed relative to IFNγ stimulation, the ultimate effect on MHCII expression was diminished.
source: As the addition of rotenone was delayed relative to IFNγ stimulation, the ultimate effect on MHCII expression was diminished (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: If rotenone was added more than 4 hr after IFNγ, negligible inhibition was observed by 24 hr.
source: If rotenone was added more than 4 hr after IFNγ, negligible inhibition was observed by 24 hr, indicating that early events were preferentially impacted by rotenone.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data showing timing-dependent effects of rotenone.

claim: The relative effect of rotenone addition over time was nearly identical in sgIrf1 and sgNTC cells.
source: While the level of MHCII induction was reduced in the absence of IRF1, the relative effect of rotenone addition over time was nearly identical in sgIrf1 and sgNTC cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing rotenone effects in IRF1-deficient and control cells.

claim: Mitochondrial function preferentially impacts the initial transcriptional response to IFNγ upstream of IRF1.
source: Thus, mitochondrial function appeared to preferentially impact the initial transcriptional response to IFNγ upstream of IRF1.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing similar rotenone effects in IRF1-deficient and control cells.

claim: Phosphorylation of JAK2 Y1007/8, STAT1-Y701, and STAT1-S727 was both delayed and reduced in sgNdufa1 cells compared to sgNTC cells following IFNγ treatment.
source: While we detected robust phosphorylation of JAK2 Y1007/8, STAT1-Y701, and STAT1-S727 over time following IFNγ treatment in sgNTC cells, phosphorylation at all three sites was both delayed and reduced across the time course in sgNdufa1 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The loss of complex I function inhibits receptor proximal signal transduction events.
source: We conclude that the loss of complex I function inhibits receptor proximal signal transduction events.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from immunoblot data showing reduced phosphorylation of signaling molecules in complex I-deficient cells.

claim: Rotenone and oligomycin inhibited the induction of MHCII by IFNγ in both macrophages and dendritic cells.
source: In both macrophages and in DCs, the induction of MHCII by IFNγ was inhibited by rotenone and oligomycin (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Rotenone and oligomycin only repressed the further induction of MHCII by IFNγ in dendritic cells, which basally express MHCII.
source: Unlike macrophages, murine DCs basally express MHCII and these inhibitors only repressed the further induction by IFNγ (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 7A and B.

claim: Inhibition of complex I in macrophages completely abolished antigen-specific T cell stimulation.
source: In macrophages, T cell stimulation relied on pretreatment of the APC with IFNγ as a macrophage line lacking the Ifngr1 gene was unable to support T cell activation. Similarly, inhibition of complex I in macrophages completely abolished antigen-specific T cell stimulation (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell activation assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Rotenone treatment of dendritic cells abrogated the IFNγ-dependent increase in T cell stimulation.
source: Regardless, rotenone treatment of DCs abrogated the IFNγ-dependent increase in T cell stimulation (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell activation assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: There is strong correlation between complex I activity in the APC population and T cell stimulatory activity.
source: In agreement with our chemical inhibition studies, we found strong correlation between complex I activity in the APC population and T cell stimulatory activity (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell activation assay data using mixed populations of complex I-deficient and control cells shown in Figures 7D and E.

claim: The IFNγ-dependent augmentation of T cell stimulatory activity depends on complex I function in both macrophages and dendritic cells.
source: Together, these data confirm that the IFNγ-dependent augmentation of T cell stimulatory activity depends on complex I function in both macrophages and DCs.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from T cell activation assays in both macrophages and DCs.

claim: Unbiased genetic analyses can reveal a multitude of unexpected cellular regulators for well-characterized processes such as IFNγ signaling.
source: Our study demonstrates that unbiased genetic analyses can reveal a multitude of unexpected cellular regulators, even for a well-characterized process such as IFNγ signaling.
evidence: The claim is a general conclusion drawn from the CRISPR screen results.

claim: The activity of the IFNγ receptor complex and subsequent transcriptional activation depends on mitochondrial function in both mouse and human myeloid cells.
source: We report that the activity of the IFNγ receptor complex and subsequent transcriptional activation depends on mitochondrial function in both mouse and human myeloid cells.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion drawn from experiments in both mouse and human cells.

claim: Experimental perturbation of respiration inhibits the capacity of both macrophages and DCs to stimulate T cells.
source: Experimental perturbation of respiration inhibits the capacity of both macrophages and DCs to stimulate T cells, identifying mitochondrial function as a central point where local signals are integrated to determine APC function.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion drawn from T cell activation assays.

claim: IFNγ stimulation increases oxygen consumption and glycolytic activity in macrophages.
source: Both our work and others report that IFNγ stimulation alters macrophage metabolism. We found that IFNγ stimulation increases oxygen consumption and glycolytic activity, and previous studies found that this treatment mediates a gradual shift to aerobic glycolysis that might be related to a reduction in mTORC1 activity (Wang et al., 2018; Su et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse metabolic data and cites previous literature.

claim: Mitochondrial respiration is required for IFNγ signaling.
source: While the overall effect of IFNγ on cellular metabolism appears to be complex and change over time, our genetic data unequivocally reveal that mitochondrial respiration is required for IFNγ signaling.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from CRISPR screen data and validation experiments.

claim: Blocking complex III, IV, or V reduces IFNγ responses, but not to the same magnitude as complex I inhibition.
source: Further chemical inhibitor studies showed that blocking complex III, IV, or V (ATP synthase) does reduce IFNγ responses, but not to the same magnitude as complex I inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing effects of different ETC inhibitors.

claim: Complex I-dependent regeneration of NAD+ is the most likely regulator of IFNγ signaling.
source: These observations indicate that the reduction state of the quinone pool and ATP generation does not regulate IFNγ responses in our system. Instead, our data indicate that complex I-dependent regeneration of NAD+ is the most likely regulator of IFNγ signaling.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from differential effects of various metabolic inhibitors.

claim: NAD+ synthesis via either the de novo or salvage pathway is necessary for a variety of macrophage functions.
source: Indeed, NAD+ synthesis via either the de novo or salvage pathway is necessary for a variety of macrophage functions (Cameron et al., 2019; Venter et al., 2014; Minhas et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Inhibition of NAD+ synthesis reduces the abundance of phospho-STAT1 by disrupting a direct interaction with TET1 in hepatocellular carcinoma cells.
source: Very recent work demonstrates an important role for NAD+ in STAT1 activation and PD-L1 induction by IFNγ in hepatocellular carcinoma cells (Lv et al., 2021). In this setting, inhibition of NAD+ synthesis reduces the abundance of phospho-STAT1 by disrupting a direct interaction with the ten-eleven translocation methylcytosine dioxygenase 1 (TET1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: TET1 is expressed at very low levels in macrophages and splenic DCs.
source: It remains unclear if a similar interaction occurs in the myeloid cells that are the focus of our work, as TET1 is expressed at very low levels in macrophages and splenic DCs (Heng et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to gene expression data.

claim: Both NAD+ synthesis and its regeneration via mitochondrial respiration contribute to the IFNγ response in diverse cell types.
source: Regardless, these observations suggest that both NAD+ synthesis and its regeneration via mitochondrial respiration contribute to the IFNγ response in diverse cell types.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from comparing results across different studies and cell types.

claim: T cell activation required mitochondrial respiration in the APC.
source: In the APC setting, we found that T cell activation required mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell activation assay data.

claim: Unstimulated DCs basally express similar levels of MHCII as IFNγ-stimulated macrophages but are unable to productively present antigen to T cells.
source: For example, unstimulated DCs basally express similar levels of MHCII as IFNγ-stimulated macrophages but are unable to productively present antigen to T cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of MHCII expression and T cell activation data between DCs and macrophages.

claim: Additional aspects of antigen processing, presentation, or co-stimulation are IFNγ- and complex I-dependent.
source: This observation suggests that additional aspects of antigen processing, presentation, or co-stimulation are IFNγ- and complex I-dependent.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion inferred from the observation that DCs with similar MHCII levels differ in T cell activation capacity.

claim: TLR stimulation has been shown to inhibit subsequent IFNγ responses via a number of target gene-specific mechanisms.
source: For example, TLR stimulation has been shown to inhibit subsequent IFNγ responses via a number of target gene-specific mechanisms (Benson and Ernst, 2009; Fortune et al., 2004; Kincaid et al., 2007; Su et al., 2020; Jang and Javadov, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TLR stimulation results in the disassembly of the ETC.
source: However, TLR stimulation also results in the disassembly of the ETC (Su et al., 2020; Jang and Javadov, 2020), which our observations predict to inhibit STAT1 phosphorylation and IFNγ signaling at the level of the receptor complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fundamental metabolic programs contribute to the integration of activation signals by APC and influence the ultimate priming of an immune response.
source: More generally, our work suggests that fundamental metabolic programs contribute to the integration of activation signals by APC and influence the ultimate priming of an immune response.
evidence: The claim is a general conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: IFNγ mediates complex effects via binding to a heterodimeric surface receptor.
source: IFNγ mediates these complex effects via binding to a heterodimeric surface receptor (Bousoik and Montazeri Aliabadi, 2018; Garcia-Diaz et al., 2017; Ealick et al., 1991; Pestka et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing the IFNγ receptor.

claim: The subunits of the IFNγ receptor complex, IFNGR1 and IFNGR2, assemble once IFNGR1 is bound by its ligand.
source: The subunits of the complex, IFNGR1 and IFNGR2, assemble once IFNGR1 is bound by its ligand (Blouin and Lamaze, 2013; Lasfar et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing receptor assembly.

claim: Complex assembly promotes the phosphorylation of JAK1 and JAK2 followed by activation of STAT1.
source: Complex assembly promotes the phosphorylation of Janus kinases 1 and 2 (JAK1 and JAK2) followed by activation of the signal transducer and activation of transcription 1 (STAT1) (Meraz et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing IFNγ signaling.

claim: Phosphorylated STAT1 dimerizes and translocates to the nucleus to activate transcription of genes containing GAS promoters.
source: Phosphorylated STAT1 then dimerizes and translocates to the nucleus to activate the transcription of genes containing promoters with IFNγ-activated sequences (GAS), which includes other transcription factors such as interferon regulatory factor 1 (Irf1) that amplify the expression of a large regulon that includes T cell co-signaling molecules (Schroder et al., 2004; Lehtonen et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing IFNγ signaling.

claim: Individuals with inborn deficiencies in IFNγ signaling suffer from Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD).
source: Individuals with inborn deficiencies in IFNγ signaling, including mutations to the receptor (Newport et al., 1996; Jouanguy et al., 1996), suffer from a defect in Th1 immunity that results in an immunodeficiency termed Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD) (Alcaïs et al., 2005; Bogunovic et al., 2012; Filipe-Santos et al., 2006; Kong et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing MSMD.

claim: Antagonists of IFNγ-inducible inhibitory molecules, such as PD-L1, are the basis for checkpoint inhibitor therapies that promote T cell-mediated tumor immunity.
source: Conversely, antagonists of IFNγ-inducible inhibitory molecules, such as PD-L1, are the basis for checkpoint inhibitor therapies that effectively promote T cell-mediated tumor immunity (Schildberg et al., 2016; Garcia-Diaz et al., 2017; Sharpe, 2017; Castro et al., 2018; George et al., 2017; Gong et al., 2019; Ivashkiv, 2018; Mahoney et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on checkpoint inhibitor therapy.

claim: Microbial stimulation of PRRs on the APC induces glycolytic metabolism, which is essential for cellular activation, migration, and T cell activation.
source: In particular, microbial stimulation of PRRs on the APC induces glycolytic metabolism and this shift in catabolic activity is essential for cellular activation, migration, and CD4+ and CD8+ T cell activation (Krawczyk et al., 2010; Guak et al., 2018; Balic et al., 2020; Carneiro et al., 2018; Everts et al., 2014; Everts et al., 2012; Jha et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017 Mills et al., 2016; Jung et al., 2018; Palmieri et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018; Baardman et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2014; Mills et al., 2018; Tannahill et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on metabolic regulation of immune cells.

claim: IFNγ stimulation has been reported to induce glycolysis and suppress mTORC1 in macrophages.
source: IFNγ stimulation has been reported to induce glycolysis, suppress the target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1), and modulate both cellular metabolism and translation in macrophages (Wang et al., 2018; Su et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on IFNγ effects on metabolism.
